title: OCC’s AI Examiner Framework: How Banks’ AI Use Can Trigger Legal Liability and Supervisory Exposure
excerpt: Home. | Insights. | OCC’s AI Examiner Framework: How Banks’ AI Use Can Trigger Legal Liability and Supervisory Exposure. PDF Link. Email. LinkedIn. Twitter/X. OCC’s AI Examiner Framework: How Banks’ AI Use Can Trigger Legal Liability and Supervisory Exposure. What You Need to Know. Key takeaway # 1. Banks’ AI failures involving lending, payments, customer communications, or anti-money laundering (AML) compliance can expose banks to liability. Key takeaway # 2. Institutions should assess AI tools based on the data and systems these tools can access, the actions they can take, and the harm they could cause. Key takeaway # 3. The Framework highlights the importance of meaningful human oversight and documentation of AI use. Client Alert | 8 min read | 11. 16. 26. On November 4, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued Bulletin 2026-54 and a Supervisory Framework on Bank Use of Super Intelligence (the “Framework”), an examiner resource addressing banks’ use of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI and AI agents that can act on their own. The Framework creates no new legal requirements or supervisory expectations, and the OCC states that banks are not expected to use it to assess their own AI use or risk management. Importantly, it identifies as higher risk several AI uses common for banks that are already governed by binding law, such as moving money, making credit decisions, and communicating with customers. A failure in any of those uses could trigger legal liability. Institutions that rely on AI for these tasks should consider the following:. Higher-risk AI failures may implicate laws already binding on the bank. Using AI does not change the bank’s existing legal obligations or the standards for a violation. Errors in AI-enabled customer communications or AML alert disposition may nevertheless result in breaches of applicable consumer protection laws or Bank Secrecy Act requirements. Productivity-enhancing tools may warrant higher-risk treatment. AI coding assistants and compliance tools can affect customer accounts or production systems. Their risk depends on what data they can access and change and their role in decisions. Banks may need to substantiate the human oversight on which assessments of their AI use cases rely. Approval and intervention records can help show whether oversight was effective. Purpose statements and system activity records may be needed to assess whether an agent stayed within its authority. AI control weaknesses may draw supervisory attention without necessarily warranting a matter requiring attention (MRA). Examiners may raise governance or control concerns, but whether a weakness warrants an MRA depends on the applicable agency’s standards for legal violations and safety-and-soundness deficiencies. A departure from the Framework alone does not establish grounds for an MRA. Structure and Risk Tiering. The Framework — which employs the Administration’s preferred phrase “super intelligence,” or SI, to refer to AI — organizes 16 components under six pillars: purpose, risk, control, oversight, resilience, and assurance. It contemplates more intensive controls where the potential consequences of an agent’s failure or misuse are greater and provides illustrative risk-tier definitions. And it applies to generative and agentic AI, which the OCC’s prior April 2026 interagency model risk management guidance expressly excluded. The examples below are illustrative, not mandatory classifications. The OCC has instructed examiners to tailor reviews to the bank’s size, complexity, and risk profile and the nature and consequences of its AI uses. Tier. Illustrative profile. Illustrative use cases. title: BioCAtch Launches AI Detection Tool to Identify Automated Agents in Online Banking
excerpt: By Noli Cajes Published: Nov 11 2026, 1:02 PM GMT. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp. Fraud prevention company BioCatch launched a new artificial intelligence (AI) detection tool on Tuesday, 10 November, designed to identify automated agents interacting with digital banking platforms. The technology aims to help financial institutions distinguish human users from AI agents and identify potentially suspicious activity before money is transferred. The tool, called BioCatch AiRE (Agentic AI Risk Essentials), monitors online banking sessions to detect AI-driven interactions in real time. According to the company, the system can identify agents acting on behalf of legitimate account holders or malicious actors, allowing banks to assess potential risks. BioCatch AiRE Monitors AI Activity in Banking Sessions. BioCatch AiRE uses behavioural analysis to identify automated agents navigating digital banking platforms. The system examined unusual interaction patterns, synthetic inputs, browser permissions and the infrastructure associated with AI agents. It also considers whether an agent has identified itself during a session. The technology continuously monitors user activity rather than relying solely on individual transactions. BioCatch said the approach allows financial institutions to assess agent behaviour throughout a banking session. Banks can use these findings to determine whether automated activity requires further investigation. The company said its detection capabilities extend to cloud-based agents, including Muse. Existing BioCatch customers can access the technology through their current integrations without introducing an entirely separate. However, the announcement did not provide independent testing results demonstrating the tool's detection accuracy. Related. The findings suggest that identifying AI-driven activity is becoming an important consideration for financial institutions. However, the survey responses reflect reported experiences and expectations rather than independently verified attack statistics. BioCatch also reported that nearly half of the AI agent interactions detected in its customer sessions occurred during account opening. Other activity appeared during account logins, account management and financial transactions. These included electronic fund transfers, wire transfers and faster payments. title: UOB to deploy A*Star AI model Meralion for customer interactions
excerpt: UOB to deploy A*Star AI model Meralion for customer interactions. The multilingual solution will help bank’s relationship managers better understand and engage with clients. Summarise. Benjamin Cher. Published Wed, Nov 18, 2026 · 12:30 PM. The AI model supports multilingual processing across seven languages in South-east Asia including English, Malay, Thai, Vietnamese and Mandarin. PHOTO: ST. [SINGAPORE] UOB announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) that it is deploying an artificial intelligence solution developed by the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*Star) to support customer interactions. Based on the Meralion AI model, the multilingual solution will help UOB’s relationship managers (RMs) better understand and engage with customers, as well as provide advice across Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam. The initial phase will be rolled out under UOB’s Project Aura, the bank’s programme to scale AI adoption and foster a culture in which employees are empowered to use AI. One of the programme’s priority domains is RMs. Leong Yung Chee, chief financial officer of UOB, said: “We want to apply AI with purpose, and we see potential for this solution to help our RMs better understand customers, navigate language and cultural nuances, and provide clearer, more relevant guidance. ”. The AI model supports multilingual processing across seven languages in South-east Asia: English, Malay, Thai, Vietnamese, Mandarin and dialects such as Cantonese and Hokkien. The solution supports RMs by interpreting customers’ questions across different languages and accents. It also provides prompts containing relevant information, such as key product details and risk disclosures, to complement RMs’ judgment and help them have more relevant conversations. title: Regulators Converge on Twin Compliance Challenges From AI Agents
excerpt: Regulators Converge on Twin Compliance Challenges From AI Agents. By PYMNTS | November 17, 2026. |. Comments by financial officials on opposite sides of the world Monday (Nov. 16) suggest regulators are converging on the need to address two challenges posed by agentic AI: how to ensure institutions remain accountable for agents they deploy, and how institutions can determine whether agents acting for customers have authority to move money or make financial decisions. Remarks by Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr and officials at a regulatory forum in Hong Kong show those concerns gaining urgency as artificial intelligence moves from generating recommendations to executing actions. The emerging debate concerns how institutions establish consent, constrain autonomy and intervene when automated systems go wrong. Speaking at an international conference on AI in finance in Milan, Barr said major banks were encountering agents attempting actions in retail customer accounts without being able to verify their authenticity, customer consent or alignment with instructions. He did not identify the banks or quantify the incidents. The Fed official called for strict authentication, explicit verification of consent for specific actions and technical controls limiting agents’ capabilities. His remarks also highlighted a challenge that extends beyond banks’ internal technology. Customers can introduce autonomous systems into financial relationships before institutions have reliable ways to recognize their authority. He also warned that agents could accelerate deposit withdrawals during periods of stress. Systems monitoring interest-rate differences or signs of instability could transfer funds automatically, potentially compressing bank runs into minutes and overwhelming conventional liquidity management and regulatory intervention. In Hong Kong, officials approached the same problem through institutional accountability and emerging supervisory arrangements. The South China Morning Post reported that regulators and industry leaders discussed market volatility, cybersecurity and other risks at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum. Financial Secretary Paul Chan’s speech made clear that institutions deploying agents, and the people overseeing them, retain responsibility. “An algorithm has no license to lose and no reputation to protect. The institution has both,” Chan said. Banks would need to establish who an agent is, what it is authorized to do and how a person can intervene. Chan pointed to Project SAGE , an initiative launched by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority earlier this month to develop agentic finance. The project examines agent identity and delegated authority, interoperability standards, and legal issues including liability, governance and consumer protection. Potential applications span consumer payments, corporate procurement and treasury management, and payments between machines. The institutional side of the challenge is equally critical. In separate remarks on Nov. 2, Securities and Futures Commission CEO Julia Leung acknowledged that human review of every intermediate step would be unrealistic. The SFC plans principles-based guidance for applications with greater autonomy. Leung outlined a graduated approach. Reversible, low-impact internal processes could receive greater autonomy, while client advice, portfolio decisions and market execution require stronger safeguards. Testing should establish whether firms can reconstruct decisions, explain outcomes and determine accountability. That approach reflects agents’ capacity to compound errors over multiple steps, or take unauthorized actions and disrupt other firms unintentionally. Human oversight must remain effective even when humans cannot approve every action, she said. Adoption figures underscore the need to distinguish current agentic deployment from ambition. title: Singapore to deploy AI to fight scams, boost business lending
excerpt: Singapore to deploy AI to fight scams, boost business lending. SINGAPORE : Singapore is setting out three artificial intelligence missions spanning financial crime, business lending and AI-agent transactions as it expands the technology’s use in finance, deputy prime minister Gan Kim Yong said. Five banks are already pooling transaction data so AI can spot scam patterns that individual lenders may miss, while the Monetary Authority of Singapore plans a study early next year for a shared detection system, Gan said in his keynote address at the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. “Scams are not confined within the boundary of one bank,” Gan, who also chairs the MAS, said. “A victim’s money can pass through several institutions within minutes. ”. The finance industry, which accounts for about 14% of Singapore’s economy and employs roughly 200,000 people, is becoming a test case for how far AI can be built into a major financial centre without undermining jobs, operations or trust. The push comes as some US banks block outside AI agents from moving customers’ money over concerns about security, control and who is responsible when something goes wrong. Gan also addressed new US rules on remote access to advanced chips, which require licenses to export them to five countries, including Singapore. The government is working with affected companies to assess the impact and engaging US authorities on how to maintain access, he said. “We value our international reputation, and we do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent or violate the laws of other countries in their international business activities,” Gan said. “We will act against those who flout our laws. ”. The latest initiatives are part of National AI Missions announced by prime minister Lawrence Wong in February, with financial services among four areas targeted for wider use of the technology. Twenty-three banks, insurers and asset managers have pledged to train more than 80,000 Singapore employees in AI skills by 2028 as firms study how jobs and tasks will change. For financial crime, MAS plans to use lessons from the five-bank trial to design a shared system that can identify suspicious activity across institutions. The first phase will focus on Singapore, though Gan said there may eventually be opportunities to work with other jurisdictions as scams cross borders. The financing mission, meanwhile, will test whether more data can help lenders assess smaller companies and startups that may lack long credit histories or assets to use as security. AI could eventually identify when a viable business needs funding and alert it to suitable options before it applies. Singapore will also test AI agents that can make payments or purchases on behalf of people and companies, potentially speeding up transactions and enabling new forms of machine-led commerce. “However, greater autonomy must come with clear responsibility and accountability,” Gan said. The systems would operate within defined limits, with firms remaining accountable for actions taken on their behalf.

title: Pocketnest Patents Conversational AI in Banking
excerpt: Proprietary architecture lets credit unions scale high-touch member guidance and wallet share—without sharing sensitive data with public LLMs. EAST LANSING, Mich. , Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Pocketnest, the embedded financial wellness platform that brings whole financial life guidance into digital banking, today announced two new patents protecting the proprietary AI architecture behind Birdie, its conversational financial guidance engine. The patents reinforce Pocketnest's position as a core technology partner for credit unions transitioning from transactional digital apps to proactive, relationship-driven hubs. "Members expect intuitive, ChatGPT-like convenience, but credit unions can't compromise on privacy, compliance, or trust," said Jessica Willis, CEO and founder, Pocketnest. "Our patented engine enables credit unions to scale high-touch, relationship-based financial planning to each member, right inside the digital channels they already use. ". Birdie translates conversational prompts into workflows targeted to agents specializing in net worth, budgeting, debt payoff, college savings, estate planning, insurance, tax planning, investments, and retirement. The newly patented architecture powers three core capabilities:. Intent-Driven Need Detection: Identifies the "question behind the question" to uncover unmet financial needs. Specialized Multi-Agent Routing: Directs inquiries to domain-specific AI agents for accurate, actionable milestone planning. Walled-Garden Data Governance : Combines connected account data with member goals inside a closed, credit union-controlled perimeter—ensuring zero data leakage to public third-party LLMs. "Members don't always ask the question they really mean, and off-the-shelf AI just answers what's on the screen," said Chris Wascha, chief technology officer, Pocketnest. "We patented a different approach. Our system looks at each question alongside the member's past conversations to work out what they're actually asking. Then it hands the question to a Pocketnest-built AI agent that specializes in that topic and can only see the data it's allowed to see. For credit unions, that means better answers and tighter control over member data. ". By pairing behavioral science with protected, domain-specific AI, Pocketnest helps credit unions boost member lifetime value, deepen community trust, and uncover automated cross-sell opportunities without scaling branch staff or operational spend. To learn how Pocketnest helps credit unions scale personalized member guidance, visit pocketnest. com. Pocketnest, Inc. ™ is an embedded financial guidance platform for financial institutions and the platforms that serve them. Using context from across the whole financial life, behavioral science, connected data, and institution-controlled technology, Pocketnest turns financial complexity into manageable next steps and trusted connections. Its white-label experience helps credit unions, banks, and financial professionals provide more relevant support inside the relationships people already trust. Pocketnest CUSO is an NCUA-registered credit union service organization and was acquired in 2025 by Reseda Group—a wholly owned CUSO of MSU Federal Credit Union—in partnership with Maps Credit Union. title: What it takes to build the AI-native modern bank
excerpt: FUTURE OF FINANCE 2026. What it takes to build the AI-native modern bank. Building an AI-infused engine for innovation, simplification and modernisation will create sustained advantage. Summarise. The goal is a radically different model of banking, characterised by highly personalised customer engagement, hyper-responsive product management, and structurally transformed operations. IMAGE: PIXABAY. Steven Breeden, Vitor D'Agnoluzzo, Joseph Edwin, Daria Huang. Published Wed, Nov 18, 2026 · 07:00 AM. COMPETITIVE advantage and performance in banking have long hinged on how effectively institutions use technology and data. Artificial intelligence represents the next step-change, reshaping how banks develop products, manage risk and serve customers. The banks that configure their organisations to absorb and exploit each wave of advances in AI will compound their advantage. Recent discussions with more than 30 senior executives of technology-savvy global banks converged on a shared view: Building an AI-infused engine for innovation, simplification and modernisation, not simply deploying AI tools, will create sustained advantage. Moving beyond efficiency. The goal is a radically different model of banking, characterised by highly personalised customer engagement, hyper-responsive product management and structurally transformed operations. The performance profile could be dramatically different from today’s banking model, aspiring to 10 times greater productivity, 100 times more experimentation throughput, 90 per cent shorter time to market, and a 10 percentage point improvement in the cost-to-income ratio. The strategic prize does not centre on efficiency. Rather, it involves velocity in time to market and experimentation. Faster trumps slimmer. THE BUSINESS TIMES INSIGHTS. Powering Asean's Future 2026. Find out how enterprises are navigating power constraints and sustainability targets. ACCESS THE INSIGHTS. Most institutions can envision these performance goals but remain constrained by legacy estates, skills shortages, inadequate data foundations, capital allocation pressures, talent and operating model. Institutions that treat AI as a set of tools layered onto existing operations will underinvest in the changes that create enduring advantage. Banks that currently capture the most value from AI treat it as a lever for growth. An AI-native modern bank requires investment and enduring commitment across five elements. 1. Agentic experiences, products. The AI-native bank does not just improve existing customer journeys; it reimagines them from the customer’s intended outcome back to what the experience, product, and underlying process should look like when built from scratch. Hyper-personalised experiences will increasingly be orchestrated by intelligent agents rather than delivered through standardised products and predefined channels. SEE ALSO. excerpt: JPMorgan Builds One AI Model to Catch 85% More Fraud. By PYMNTS | November 17, 2026. |. Highlights. JPMorgan built a single AI model for fraud detection, payment authorization predictions and retries, trained on up to 400 billion tokens of card, ACH and wire transaction data. The model improved card fraud detection by up to 85. 5%, ACH fraud detection by 27. 4% and payment retry predictions by 22. 8% compared with the bank’s task-specific models. Seventy-one percent of financial institutions plan to build new fraud systems themselves, up from 44% a year earlier, PYMNTS Intelligence found. JPMorganChase has built one artificial intelligence model to handle fraud detection, authorization prediction and payment retries, three jobs that draw on much of the same transaction data. Building a separate model for each one means teaching every model the same payment patterns again, the bank’s researchers wrote in a paper published Nov. 11. The Large Payments Model, or LPM, learns from payment records instead of text. Each transaction enters as a fixed set of fields that hold numbers, categories or short text, such as dates, postal codes and descriptions. The training data covers card payments where JPMorgan is the merchant’s acquirer, plus ACH and wire transfers. The largest version was trained on up to 400 billion tokens, the units of data a model reads. The model is already in production. It is “serving millions of transactions per day” and completes 99% of requests within 60 milliseconds, the researchers wrote. Each transaction costs less than $0. 0001 to score. Transaction History Pushes Card Fraud Gains to 85%. JPMorgan tested two versions of LPM on card payments, the researchers wrote. The first scores each transaction on its own and improved fraud detection by 62. 7% over a model built only for that task, the paper’s results table showed. The measure, average precision, tracks how well a model ranks rare fraud cases above legitimate payments, the researchers said. The second version reads up to six months of prior transactions tied to the same party. That history pushed the fraud detection gain to 85. 5%. The same model also predicts what happens to a payment after it is sent. It was 80% better at predicting which of about 100 responses a card network would return and 22. 8% better at predicting how a card network would respond to a retried payment. LPM also handled a job it was not trained for. Asked to predict whether a retried payment would eventually be approved, the model needed only a small add-on to score 0. 5% above a model built for that job, the researchers wrote. Every result is a gain over JPMorgan’s own single-task models, measured on the bank’s own card and treasury payments, the researchers said. The paper does not name those models, give their absolute scores or test LPM against a public benchmark. It includes no figures on fraud losses, false declines or cost savings. ACH Gains Reach 27% While Wires Lag. Treasury payments, meaning ACH and wire transfers, were tested differently. Fraud teams can review only so many alerts a day, so the researchers held that number fixed and measured how much more fraud the model surfaced. LPM caught 27. 4% more fraudulent ACH payments and 63. 5% more fraud by dollar value, the paper showed. Wire transfers did not see the same lift. The model caught 5. 6% more fraudulent wires and no additional dollar value, the paper found, a gap the researchers tied to wires making up a smaller share of the training data. The design has limits, the researchers said. Adding new data fields may require more training, and neither version removes the need to summarize long payment histories.
